```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment='#>', fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5)
library(suppose)
```

A fitted model is a starting point for inquiry. Suppose helps you inspect its
assumptions, explore possible outcomes, and retain your interpretation of what
those consequences mean. A model implication remains conditional on the model
and its scope; it is not a newly observed fact or automatically a causal effect.

## Begin with a provided model

You do not need a fitted model or a provider key. Three saved examples come with
Suppose. They contain actual brms predictions from synthetic data, including
coherent parameter draws and simulated future outcomes. Opening them requires
neither brms nor a Stan compiler.

```{r examples}
linear <- suppose_model_example('linear')
curved <- suppose_model_example('curved')
waiting <- suppose_model_example('waiting')
vapply(list(linear, curved, waiting), function(w) w$title, character(1))
```

- **Straight-line coating model:** a constant change in mean strength per degree.
- **Curved coating model:** the same synthetic fitting data, with a quadratic
  relationship that can turn downward. Compare it with the straight-line model.
- **Waiting-time model:** positive, skewed service waits under a lognormal model.
  It illustrates multiplicative changes and the distinction between an average
  outcome and an individual wait.

```{r open-app, eval=FALSE}
suppose_app(model = linear)
```

Passing `model = world` retains that simulation artifact in the starting inquiry,
without accepting an interpretation. **Explore this model in conversation** also
makes the selected model available and prepares a question for the composer;
it does not send a message automatically. A connected chat provider can then
discuss the predictions and assumptions.

You can also open **Model worlds** in an ordinary `suppose_app()` session, or
choose the model-world example from **Examples**. Each example tab has its own
copy of the developing inquiry.

```{r example-plot, fig.alt="Coherent draw and simulated strength outcomes from the curved coating model, compared with the increasing median prediction of the straight-line model. The models diverge outside the 20 to 40 degree fitting range."}
plot_model_world(curved, scenario = 36, comparison = linear)
```

## A short walkthrough

1. Read the scientific interpretation. Expand the formula and likelihood details
   to distinguish the author's interpretation from restrictions in the code.
2. Move the temperature from 30 to 70 degrees C. The fitting range is 20–40;
   the app identifies the move beyond that range as extrapolation.
3. Step through simulated experiments. A purple curve uses one shared parameter
   draw across all scenarios. Orange points add outcome variation under that
   same draw. The shaded intervals are pointwise 90% intervals, not a joint
   coverage guarantee for an entire curve or experiment.
4. Compare the curved and straight-line models. Their behavior diverges well
   beyond the data. The curved model can predict physically impossible negative
   strength; a locally useful shape is not automatically a global model.
5. Draft a statement, then edit it in your own words. Accept, qualify or challenge
   the interpretation, explain your reasoning, and propose an observation that
   would probe it. Retain the review and save the record before closing.

The threshold control changes the question asked of the saved predictions. It
neither refits the model nor changes a utility function. Probability estimates
are fractions of a finite set of posterior draws and have Monte Carlo error.
A zero count does not establish zero probability.

## Retain an interpretation in R

A review can relate an independently worded claim to a model without overwriting
an existing inquiry's main claim. The exact model snapshots, scenario, threshold,
shown realization and comparison summary are retained.

```{r review}
record <- elicitation_record(claim(
  'Which strength predictions deserve a direct check?',
  author = 'Example analyst'
))
implication <- claim(
  'The straight-line extrapolation needs an explicit scope limit.',
  author = 'Example analyst',
  scope = linear$scope
)
record <- record_model_implication(
  record, linear, implication,
  position = 'qualify',
  reason = 'The models disagree beyond the 20–40 degree fitting range.',
  challenge = 'Collect independent preparations at 50 and 60 degrees under a fixed protocol.',
  author = 'Example analyst',
  reviewed = TRUE,
  scenario = 36, # temperature 70 in this explicit grid
  threshold = 60,
  realization = 2,
  comparison = curved
)
record$model_implications[[1]]$summary
```

```{r roundtrip}
path <- tempfile(fileext = '.json')
write_record(record, path)
reopened <- read_record(path)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(record, reopened)))
unlink(path)
```

Use `record_model_world(record, world)` to retain a simulation artifact before
forming an interpretation. It adds no observation or acceptance.

The proposed challenge is a research question. It does not freeze a numerical
prospective test, add observations, or authorize fitting an alternative model.
External snapshots are not routed to Suppose's built-in regression-design
methods. Those methods have a different, explicitly supported model contract.

## Bring a brms model

The first adapter accepts a bounded set of univariate MCMC fits: Gaussian models
with identity or log links, and lognormal models with identity links. It supports
numeric formula terms and arithmetic transformations, including a quadratic
term. Supply all formula predictors in the scenario table and units for each;
only the plotted predictor may vary. Scientific scope must be supplied by the author. The fitting range defaults to
the observed span of the plotted predictor; an explicitly supplied range must
match it. Other predictors are held fixed at the supplied scenario settings.

```{r own-fit, eval=FALSE}
library(brms)
fit <- brm(strength ~ temperature, data = my_measurements, family = gaussian())
world <- inspect_model(
  fit,
  scenarios = data.frame(temperature = seq(20, 60, by = 2)),
  varying = 'temperature',
  units = c(temperature = 'degC'),
  outcome_units = 'MPa',
  title = 'My coating model',
  scope = 'Independent preparations under our stated protocol',
  source = 'My measurements; collection protocol and dates recorded separately',
  assumptions = 'The linear response and constant variability need checking.',
  training_range = c(20, 40),
  threshold = 60,
  lower_bound = 0,
  draws = 400,
  seed = 47
)
suppose_app(model = world)
```

The adapter uses the same posterior draw IDs for
[`posterior_epred()`](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/posterior_epred.brmsfit.html)
and [`posterior_predict()`](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/posterior_predict.brmsfit.html).
The first describes uncertainty about the expected response; the second also
includes individual-outcome variation. In the lognormal example, the expected
response includes the mean adjustment for lognormal variation, rather than
simply exponentiating the linear predictor.

The saved snapshot includes the formula, prior summary, supplied context,
scenario grid, up to 1,000 numeric fitting-data points for single-predictor models, predictive draws,
software version, seed, selected draw IDs and data/model fingerprints. It also
reports limited computational diagnostics. Low R-hat and no divergences do not
establish adequacy or scientific validity. For multiple predictors, the plot omits unadjusted fitting-data points and lists
the other predictor settings held fixed. The caller's fitted model and RNG state
are preserved. An incompatible prediction result fails without retaining a
partial snapshot.

These records contain fitting data and predictions. Treat a saved record as you
would the underlying research data when sharing it. A fingerprint detects
identity or changes; it is not an authenticity certificate.

## Rebuild the examples

The full data-generating and brms fitting script is shipped with the package and
can be downloaded from **Model source and computation** in the walkthrough.
It writes fitted models and snapshots to `model-world-examples` in your working
directory. This optional step requires brms and a working Stan toolchain and can
take several minutes.

```{r rebuild, eval=FALSE}
file.copy(
  system.file('model-worlds', 'build-model-worlds.R', package = 'suppose'),
  'build-model-worlds.R'
)
source('build-model-worlds.R')
fit <- readRDS('model-world-examples/world-linear-fit.rds')
```

Use a fresh output directory if you modify the script's models or data. Across
platforms or sampler versions, refitted draws can differ; the shipped predictions
remain fixed and inspectable.

## Boundaries of this first adapter

Group-level effects, autocorrelation, missing predictors, response additions,
smooths, distributional formulas, prior-only fits, custom Stan code, non-MCMC fits, and other likelihoods require
additional contracts. Stan and tidymodels adapters are not implemented yet.
Neither model refitting, generalized sensitivity analysis nor external-model
experiment design is implied by being able to inspect a snapshot.
